title: Idledale Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Idledale wells have a 305-foot median depth, 6.8 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $25,800-$42,500.
h1: What Wells Are Like in Idledale, Colorado
intro_html:
Buying land in Idledale means dealing with mountain bedrock, variable well depths, and a water supply that can change from one lot to the next. Records for permitted wells within 5 miles show a 305-foot median depth and a 6.8 gallon-per-minute median reported yield.

The records are useful for setting expectations, but they do not guarantee what a new hole will produce. Idledale, Genesee, Indian Hills, Morrison, Kittredge, and Golden sit in a fractured-rock setting where nearby results are valuable evidence, not a promise. Review the permit record, water rights, septic layout, and environmental history before closing.

sections.heading: Idledale well depths reflect fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
Most Idledale-area wells are drilled into unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers. The median completed depth is 305 feet, while the middle half runs from 148 to 556 feet. That spread is large enough to matter when comparing drilling bids. A shallow estimate based on one nearby well may not fit the next lot.

The depth mix shows the same variability: 18% of reported wells are under 100 feet, 27% fall from 100 to 300 feet, 32% from 300 to 600 feet, and 23% exceed 600 feet. The deepest record is 4,095 feet, although that is not a normal planning assumption. Fractured granite and gneiss produce water through cracks, so the driller may need to continue below a dry or weak zone.

sections.heading: What an Idledale well may produce
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting pump yield, the median is 6.8 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 3.0 and 10.0 gpm. That is generally a workable range for a household when the well, pressure system, storage, and demand are properly matched.

Reported results are spread across the area: 3% produce under 1 gpm, 29% are between 1 and 5 gpm, 61% between 5 and 15 gpm, and 7% exceed 15 gpm. A buyer should not treat the median as a guaranteed flow rate. Ask for the well construction report and pumping test, then confirm how the result compares with neighboring wells in Idledale, Kittredge, Genesee, or Indian Hills.

sections.heading: The Idledale water-level record is not a simple trend
sections.html:
Static water level means the depth from the ground surface down to the water when the well is not being pumped. The median for reported measurements is 100 feet, with the middle half from 48 to 180 feet. Those figures help with pump planning, but they are not the same as well depth or guaranteed available water.

By measurement decade, the median was 30 feet in the 1960s, 45 feet in the 1970s, 74 feet in the 1980s, 150 feet in the 1990s, 137 feet in the 2010s, and 125 feet in the 2020s. The series suggests water levels became deeper than early records, but it does not show a continuing decline in the latest decades. Different locations and measurement conditions limit the comparison.

sections.heading: Permit history and drillers around Idledale
sections.html:
The permit record is substantial: 4,389 permitted wells are mapped within 5 miles, 2,801 are recorded as constructed, 2,912 report total depth, and 1,299 report pump yield. Most listed uses are domestic or household at 85%; stock is 3%, irrigation is 1%, and monitoring is 6%.

Permitting was busiest in the 1990s, with 956 permits, after 721 in the 1970s and 589 in the 1980s. The newest permit year is 2025, so this is not only an historic record. The most active names are James Drilling Company, Aspen Drilling Company Inc, and Living Water Systems Inc. Verify current availability, scope, and references directly before selecting a driller.

sections.heading: Estimated cost to drill and finish an Idledale well
sections.html:
For fractured mountain bedrock, the drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot. At the 305-foot median depth, that puts the drilled hole at about $19,800-$30,500. This is the hole only, not the complete water system.

A finished well including pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,800-$42,500 at the median depth. A bid can move outside that range if the lot requires more drilling, difficult access, extra casing or grout, deeper pump setting, or longer utility trenching. Ask what happens if the hole is dry or produces less than the target yield. Also request separate prices for testing, permits, water treatment, storage, and site restoration so the comparison is meaningful.

sections.heading: Environmental and building checks before buying
sections.html:
Low yield and dry holes are the main water-supply risks in fractured mountain rock. A nearby producing well does not prove that the same fracture system crosses your building site. Review neighboring construction reports, pump tests, static levels, and any recorded history of deepening or replacement.

Water quality deserves its own investigation. Within about 10 miles, the mapped record includes 106 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 182 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These locations do not establish contamination at a particular parcel, but they are a reason to test the existing well and understand the site's position relative to mines and cleanup areas.

Before building, confirm well access, electrical service, casing and grout condition, septic setbacks, and a suitable septic replacement area. Colorado DWR permits and water-right restrictions also matter; an exempt household-use well is not permission for every type of use.

sections.heading: A practical plan for an Idledale lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's surrounding permits, not a broad county average. Compare wells in Idledale with the closest useful records in Genesee, Indian Hills, Morrison, Kittredge, and Golden, giving more weight to similar bedrock and elevation. Have a Colorado well professional review depth, yield, water level, casing, grout, and pump information before you remove an inspection condition.

For a vacant lot, confirm that a driller can reach the site and that the proposed well and septic fields can coexist with the driveway, house, drainage, and utility routes. Budget using the local median range, but keep room for a deeper hole or lower yield. If the planned use involves more than ordinary household needs, verify the permit and water-right requirements early. The goal is to prove that water, wastewater, access, and construction can all fit before buying.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Idledale, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Idledale is 305 feet. The middle half runs from 148 to 556 feet, showing substantial local variation. About 23% of reported wells exceed 600 feet, while 18% are under 100 feet. Fractured mountain bedrock means nearby wells help with planning but cannot guarantee a new well depth.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Idledale?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65-$100 per foot in fractured granite and gneiss. At the 305-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $19,800-$30,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,800-$42,500. Extra depth, difficult access, and site conditions can raise the bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Idledale?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a 6.8 gpm median, with the middle half from 3.0 to 10.0 gpm. About 3% of reported wells produce under 1 gpm, while 61% produce 5-15 gpm. These are area records, not guarantees. Review the specific well test and ask how storage and household demand are handled.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Idledale?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. The area within about 10 miles includes 106 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 182 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those mapped features do not prove a parcel is contaminated. Test the existing or new well for appropriate contaminants and review nearby mine and cleanup records.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping in Idledale wells?
faq.a: The median reported static water level was 30 feet below surface in the 1960s, 150 feet in the 1990s, 137 feet in the 2010s, and 125 feet in the 2020s. That suggests levels were deeper than in early records, but the latest series does not show a continuing decline. Different wells and measurement conditions make this a broad regional comparison.
